newsitem.title: GERMANY: Farming -- Eastern Germany must build on advantages.
newsitem.headline: Farming -- Eastern Germany must build on advantages.

text.p: East German farming has successfully mastered its transition into the European Union but it needs to exploit this stability to diversify ahead of further market liberalisation, a farm union official said.
"The region clearly has a lead in arable farming but it now needs to rebuild its livestock industries," said Helmut Born, secretary-general of the DBV pan-German farm union.
Born, who was talking to Reuters during the "Green Week" farm fair, said arable earnings were dependent on EU compensation payments, which would be cut in the years to come.
But East German livestock numbers were still falling after a post-unification collapse caused by inadequate structures.
Pig numbers at a count last December were below three million and falling, compared with 12 million before 1990.
"I hope the East German states recognise that by supporting animal rearing, they will help bring profits and new jobs in food processing, feeds and supply industries," Born said.
"We will support that process by opposing some drastic reform efforts, for instance sharp milk price cuts, in Brussels as long as eastern Germany still benefits from low wages."
Changeable weather brought sharp crop losses in 1996 and showed the need to lessen dependency on arable incomes.
The region's continental climate generates more varied crop results than the more stable sea climate in the West of Europe.
Farm sizes and profits outside this context were a success.
Average profits on East German farms in 1995-96 were 96,000 marks, up 15.7 percent from 94-95, while those in the West, at 48,000 marks, were only up by 2.4 percent, DBV data showed.
Farm sizes were much bigger in the East. Full-time farms in the West had an average 50-60 hecates under control.

In the East, family farms and small joint firms averaged 200 ha, but large joint-stock companies built from former collective farms, which account for 34 percent of the total area, had about 1,000 ha each. By comparison, the EU average is 16 ha.
Born stressed the figures should not be over-analysed because they only told part of a complex story.

While the land lease rate in the East was 90 percent, it was 47 percent in the West, offering a property cushion. A slim capital base and old debts carried over from communist times hampered investments in the East.
Most of the special transition privilages such as debt cancellations or aid payments had expired at the end of 1996.
East Germany's farm sector had shed most of its 820,000 workers and only kept 150,000, at great social cost.
Problems over land ownership are also still unresolved and overshadow the progress made in the East.
Land-privatising agencies still must settle disputes on over 1.1 million ha, a third of total arable land and forest.
The Bonn government is also fending off compensation claims by former owners of estates belonging to the Prussian nobility seized by Soviet authorities between 1945 and 1949.
"Uncertainty over possible future financial claims weighs on farming sentiment in the region," Born said.
The DBV official said 1997 should not be a bad year for German farmers -- a weaker currency would help dairy exporters and grains prices may only ease slightly.
